title: MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that most LLM-based tutoring systems for mathematics do not account for students’ emotional states, despite educational psychology research showing that affect influences motivation, engagement, and learning. The authors argue that ignoring emotions can lead to disengagement and weaker learning experiences, especially in mathematics, where frustration and anxiety are common. To address this gap, they develop and evaluate MathBuddy, an emotionally aware AI math tutor that integrates affect recognition into tutoring responses.

MathBuddy is a multimodal tutoring system that detects student emotion from both conversational text and facial expressions captured through webcam input. It maps these signals into three broad affective categories—positive, neutral, and negative—and then adjusts the tutoring strategy accordingly, using pedagogically grounded prompting for the underlying LLM tutor. The system was evaluated in two ways: automatic benchmarking on math tutoring conversations using win rate and pedagogical quality metrics across eight dimensions, and a real-time within-subject user study comparing an Emotion ON condition versus an Emotion OFF condition.

The empirical context includes 30 participants aged 15 to 55 who completed two short tutoring sessions on geometry and probability, with randomized order of emotion-aware versus non-emotion-aware conditions. Participants were largely drawn from the IT:U Interdisciplinary Transformation University Austria community, making the setting closer to a controlled digital study than a regular classroom deployment. The paper also reports creation of a small annotated dataset of 224 student utterances for text emotion recognition and evaluates facial emotion recognition components on benchmark image datasets.

The main conclusions are that incorporating student emotion modeling can improve the pedagogical quality of LLM tutor responses and enhance user experience. On automatic evaluation, the emotion-aware version of the best tutor showed a 23-point gain in win rate and a 3-point gain in overall DAMR score. In the user study, participants generally rated the emotion-aware condition more positively, and facial-expression analyses suggested longer positive emotional states under Emotion ON. However, the authors also note that emotion aggregation remains imperfect, especially for neutral states, and that additional modalities and more nuanced emotion modeling are needed in future work.

identified_tools.name: MathBuddy
identified_tools.description: An emotionally aware multimodal LLM-powered math tutoring system that detects student affect from conversational text and facial expressions, aggregates it into positive/neutral/negative states, and adapts tutoring strategy accordingly.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a math tutor that uses text- and webcam-based emotion recognition to adapt pedagogical responses, with automatic benchmark evaluation and a within-subject user study comparing emotion-aware vs non-emotion-aware conditions.

findings.finding_summary: On the MathTutorBench/MathDial-Bridge hard benchmark, the emotion-aware LearnLM-based MathBuddy variant outperformed the non-emotion-aware baseline in automatic pedagogical evaluation. The paper reports a 23-point gain in win rate (0.59 to 0.82) and a 3-point gain in overall DAMR score (0.85 to 0.88) for LearnLM+, with improvements in six of eight pedagogical dimensions.
findings.measure: Win Rate and overall Desired Annotation Match Rate (DAMR) across eight pedagogical dimensions on 327 human-annotated math tutoring conversations

findings.finding_summary: In an ablation on Qwen2.5-7B-Socratic-LM, adding emotion features alone reduced performance, but adding emotion features grounded in educational theory improved results above baseline. Reported win rates were 0.28 for QSLM, 0.21 for QSLM+emotion, and 0.37 for QSLM+emotion+ET under the simple prompt; under the complex prompt they were 0.33, 0.12, and 0.35 respectively.
findings.measure: Win Rate in ablation study comparing baseline, emotion-only, and emotion+education-theory prompting
findings.effect_size: Simple prompt: +0.09 vs baseline for emotion+ET; Complex prompt: +0.02 vs baseline for emotion+ET

findings.finding_summary: In a within-subject user study, participants reported generally higher average satisfaction scores on a 15-item post-interaction questionnaire when MathBuddy used emotion-aware adaptation (Emotion ON) than when emotions were not used to guide responses (Emotion OFF). The paper interprets this as a more positive perceived learning experience under the emotion-aware condition.
findings.measure: 15-item Likert-scale post-interaction questionnaire on engagement, perceived support, empathy, coherence, and related learning experience dimensions

findings.finding_summary: Participants showed significantly longer average durations of positive facial expressions in the emotion-aware condition than in the non-adaptive condition. Mean positive-expression duration was 1.14s (SD=0.87) in Emotion ON versus 0.93s (SD=0.87) in Emotion OFF, with a Wilcoxon paired test p=.046; negative and neutral durations were not significantly different.
findings.measure: Mean duration of positive, neutral, and negative facial emotion states during tutoring sessions
findings.effect_size: Positive emotion duration difference: 1.14s vs 0.93s; p=.046

findings.finding_summary: MathBuddy's real-time multimodal emotion aggregation achieved 60% overall accuracy against participant-reviewed gold annotations. Classwise performance was uneven: Negative precision/recall/F1 = 0.57/0.98/0.72, Neutral = 0.71/0.15/0.25, and Positive = 0.79/0.41/0.54, indicating especially poor recall for neutral states.
findings.measure: Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 of aggregated multimodal emotion detection compared with participant-corrected labels

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical system paper with automatic benchmark evaluation and a within-subject user study, but it is not a K-12 RCT/QED and relies heavily on automatic pedagogical metrics and user-experience measures. Sample sizes are modest and many learning outcome statistics are descriptive rather than causal achievement effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful positive effects on benchmark pedagogical metrics, including a large win-rate improvement (+0.23) and statistically significant gains in positive affect duration. However, direct math learning gains from pre/post tests are not clearly quantified, so overall impact is promising but only modestly evidenced.
